precepts.why:
“Man’s goings are of the Lord; how can a man then understand his own way?” Our days are ordered by God. Job's situation was not his own doing: the whole purpose of it is Satan trying to prove that a man put through certain things will curse God, and that was not Job's case. Job knows he is not in the sin these brothers claim; he contests everything they say. “My friends scorn me: but mine eye poureth out tears unto God.” His witness is in heaven and his record is on high.

Since a man's goings are of the Most High, we must move with purpose knowing this. What Job is going through can be applied to our captivity in this country today; our goings here are of the Lord too.

precepts.text: The way of a man is not in himself; it is not in man that walks to direct his own steps, confirming that Job's trials and our walk are under the hand of the Most High.

What he is going through can be applied to our captivity in this country today.

precepts.why:
“O Lord, I know that the way of man is not in himself: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps.” It is not in man to direct his own steps. This confirms that Job's trials and our walk are under the hand of the Most High.

Job knows he is not in the sin these brothers claim and contests everything they say; his witness is in heaven and his record is on high. He understands the whole purpose of his situation is Satan trying to prove that a man put through certain things will curse God, and that was not Job's case. His steps were being directed. “When a few years are come, then I shall go the way whence I shall not return.” What he is going through can be applied to our captivity in this country today: the way is not in us, it is under his hand.

points: Job tells his friends he has heard many such things, and calls them miserable comforters, all of them. Their company is miserable and they are no help.

note.label: Job 16: Miserable Comforters Are Ye All

points: He asks whether vain words shall have an end. He says if their souls were in his soul's stead, he could heap up words against them and shake his head at them too, but instead he would strengthen them with his mouth and the moving of his lips would ease their grief.

note.label: Job 16: Miserable Comforters Are Ye All

points: Job says though he speak, his grief is not eased, and though he forbear, he is not eased. The word "asswaged" here means to lessen the intensity, unable to ease, so it reads that his grief is not eased and by forbearing what is he eased.

note.label: Job 16: Miserable Comforters Are Ye All

points: He says God has made him weary and made desolate all his company, and filled him with wrinkles which is a witness against him, his leanness rising up and bearing witness to his face.

note.label: Job 16: Miserable Comforters Are Ye All

points: Job describes God tearing him in wrath and gnashing upon him with His teeth, his enemy sharpening his eyes upon him. Men gape upon him with their mouths and smite him upon the cheek reproachfully, gathering themselves together against him.

note.label: Job 16: Miserable Comforters Are Ye All

points: God has delivered him to the ungodly and turned him over into the hands of the wicked. He was at ease but was broken asunder, taken by the neck and shaken to pieces, set up as a mark for God's archers. God cleaves his reins asunder, pours out his gall upon the ground, breaks him with breach upon breach, and runs upon him like a giant.

note.label: Job 16: Miserable Comforters Are Ye All

points: Job has sewed sackcloth upon his skin and defiled his horn in the dust. His face is foul with weeping and on his eyelids is the shadow of death.

note.label: Job 16: Miserable Comforters Are Ye All

points: Yet this is not for any injustice in his hands, and his prayer is pure.

note.label: Job 16: Miserable Comforters Are Ye All

points: Job cries out for the earth not to cover his blood and for his cry to have no resting place. His witness is in heaven and his record is on high.

note.label: Job 16: Miserable Comforters Are Ye All

points: His friends scorn him, but his eye pours out tears unto God. He longs that one might plead for a man with God as a man pleads for his neighbor. When a few years are come, then he shall go the way whence he shall not return.
